translations.text: March 7. The martyrdom of the holy and glorious martyrs newly revealed.
Theodore, Constantine, Theophilus, Callistus, Bassoes, and their companions.
He spoke about the sufferings of the martyrs: Let us who love the martyrs press forward, receiving grace from them.
Come, then, and stand today before the martyrs newly revealed to us.
And let us consider the good things they gathered together.
But for me, O most pure and Christ-loving audience, [?] the trials of martyrdom [?].
Yet I am held by love, or rather by fear, and truly I have been moved to wonder:
How, having scorned everything, they turned to God, the Master and Creator, away from such great glory and rank,
which they held in this world, and which were exceedingly splendid; for nothing [?], having broken away,
but having scorned everything, they received eternal salvation. For they asked the Master for this grace.
And eagerly they received crowns, the labors of martyrdom [?], and chose to walk in heaven,
rather than enjoy the fleeting pleasure of sin. They knew Christ the Master
very well, and, more than that, they were known by him. They asked him for grace from heaven,
and received twofold in return for one. They loved holy things more than earthly things, and received good things.
They received what they loved: incorruptible things rather than corruptible things, and obtained them at once.
They desired to be honored forever, and they rejoice with the angels. They made a bargain through heavenly deeds,
and gained twice as much. They scorned earthly military service and obtained heavenly service.
O wondrous and most glorious deeds! Who would not marvel at this fervent faith?
How joyfully they dared to face suffering! How unhesitatingly they approached martyrdom!
Now, then, let us break off this discourse and turn to the martyrs, faithfully recounting the course of their conduct:
how they were brought into the land of the Saracens, how they lived, and how their martyrdom came about.
Listen, O lovers of God, honorable and good audience. Open the eyes of your hearts,
and receive this quietly. Let the beloved forty-two martyrs come and walk with us in spirit.
For although they were martyred without us, we believe that they are with us in spirit. Let us [?] the account before the spectators,
joining it together. Theophilus, who reigns over us, assembled an army and marched out against the impure Saracens.
And having done this, he obtained what he desired, having plundered the glorious cities of the godless Saracens,
where the family of the Amir al-Mu'minin also lived. They call the prince of their council Amir al-Mu'minin,
for he is also called the chief counselor. He returned from there,
bringing us trophies of victory and much plunder of various kinds. After these things had happened,
the evildoer rose against the Christians, and, having mustered all his troops,
the following year he came to the beloved city of Amorium, intending to plunder it.
For the city was so beloved and glorious
that it was reputed to be second only to Constantinople. So when he came to the city,
the aforementioned foul Amir al-Mu'minin began to wage war against it. And as these things were happening,
sometimes fighting and sometimes using deceit, he captured the city. Once the godless man had entered the city,
he acted as a godless man would. Oh, the calamities! Who can recount
the sorrow and sighing and weeping of the people living in that city? A father saw his son being slaughtered,
and a son his father, and a mother her daughter, and a daughter her mother, a master his slaves, and slaves their master, one friend another,
and one brother another, and the rest in turn. Simply put, some were slaughtered, others burned, and others strangled.
Thus they suffered the Lord's death. And now there was nowhere any rest, nowhere any relief,
nowhere anything life-giving, but everywhere death, everywhere sorrow,
everywhere weeping, everywhere sighing, everywhere slaughter, everywhere blood,
everywhere tears, with no one to show pity and no one to show mercy.
Oh, the anguish! Oh, the calamities! Oh, the weeping! Oh, the slaughter! Oh, those lawless bodies!
How those savage men defile the air with their foul deeds! The godless men, seeing the lawless slaughter,
also came upon the newly radiant champions of the true faith, who through the Spirit of the Lord were golden streams,
lovely flowers for Christians, traveling laborers, most excellent martyrs.
And having bound their hands and feet, they ordered them to be sent to the land of the Saracens,
to be shut up in prison and closely guarded, together with a countless multitude of Christians.
Oh, what a wonder! How the lawless man binds the free! How a slave to sin makes others slaves!
who are workers of righteousness. After being bound, they went away in great sorrow and distress.
Along the way, this vile Commander of the Faithful killed whomever he wished.
Others he gave to his nobles as slaves, and others he sent to prison.
The noble martyrs went into the land of Syria, suffering deprivation and being cast into prison.
For you know, brothers, how captives suffer. While they were in prison, they urged one another to pray to the Lord,
so that they would not stumble in any way and fall away from their faith. For this was what the deceiver had in mind:
that they should merely taste his food and share in his faith.
If they did this, they would be deemed worthy of honorable and great gifts.
While he had this in mind, seven years passed in prison,
as they kept their faith pure and firm. Then the evildoer, urged on by his father the devil,
commanded them to surrender to him and join him, or, if they refused to submit, to be condemned to death.
He gave an order to one of his nobles, saying, “Go into the prison,
and bring before me tomorrow the notable men you have there, who are called Christians.”
That cruel servant went, entered the prison, and ordered them to come out.
When they had come out, he ordered them to be bound with iron chains. Once they were bound,
the unconquered soldiers of Christ went rejoicing to the evildoer.
When they had been led into the court of the Commander of the Faithful, he was informed about them.
The messenger said, “Look, these men stand before you.”
He asked him, “Will they submit to our law or not?” The servant said, “I do not know, my lord.”
Then he opened his mouth and said, “Though we have devised every possible means, we have been unable to persuade them
to renounce their Christ and join us. Now go and declare this to them:
‘The ruler of all Syria says this to you: Of the two choices set before you,
which are opposed to one another, choose one:
either renounce Christ and rejoice with us, or, if you refuse to submit, die by the sword today.’” When the valiant soldiers heard this,
who were truly workers of Christ, as if with one mouth,
And they said with one voice, “May we never deny the heavenly King.
Rather, we worship the Trinity, one in essence and undivided.
But we oppose you, Emperor, and do not obey your commands. For we have learned from the holy Scriptures to obey God and not princes.”
When the deceiver heard this, he blazed with anger and, shouting loudly, ordered that the next morning, at the River Tigris,
they should assemble where they had been before, and that the trial should take place there in the deceiver’s presence.
The saints made the journey from the place mentioned to the river,
from the ninth hour until dawn. And when both parties drew near the river,
these martyrs were bound, while that deceitful and untamed dog,
traveling by water, ordered them to be shut up together in a prison. Then he left the boat and came to them on horseback.
He stopped and said to his servants, “Bring me one of them, so that perhaps at least he will agree to obey me
and will make the others agree.” They brought forward the honorable vessel and pillar of the martyrs, the firm rock of faith,
the invincible Theodore, the glorious [?] protospatharios, another eunuch, emulating the eunuch of Candace,
who does not point out water to Philip so that he may be baptized and believe in the Lord—for he already had a share in that—
but is to shed his blood and be baptized in it. When he had taken his stand, the ruler said to the martyr through an interpreter, “Obey me, man,
and abandon Christianity and become like us, so that you may receive great honor from me.
I will give you great wealth, and you will not be condemned to death. For you are a eunuch and have no concerns for a wife or
children, but are chaste. And just as you have lived in your own land,
so you will live with me, with added benefits, and I will make you one of my nobles.”
The martyr answered through the interpreter, saying, “May I never, you untamed dog,
deny my Christ, the heavenly King, and join the demons.” When he answered thus with confidence,
the interpreter was unable to report the insults and reproaches to the crafty Commander of the Faithful.
He approached and began to admonish the martyr, saying, “Obey me and the emperor, man, so that you do not die.”
Christ’s martyr answered, saying, “You wretched, fainthearted man, you worker of lawlessness!
If I did not submit to your emperor when he urged me, how am I to submit to you?”
Then the interpreter too became angry, and his emperor asked him what the martyr had said to him.
He answered, “He insults you and reproaches you, O king.” And the deceitful man became angry,
and, burning with rage and roaring like a lion against the righteous man, he ordered his honored head to be cut off with a sword,
so that where he had given his answer, there his body also met its end. For the workers of lawlessness were unrestrained.
They untied his belt and tied up his hair, and, tearing
his clothes from his neck down to his feet, they struck him with a sword. And so he gave up his soul to the Lord.
After he had been beheaded, the true worker of Christ lay on the ground like a bright star that had come down from heaven to earth.
Still choking with rage at the martyr’s endurance,
he said, “Bring me here cruel men from the land of Ethiopia, with swords, to cut the others to pieces.”
And he brought in his advisers and said to them, “Did you see the endurance of that ungodly man?”
They said, “We saw it and were amazed.” “Then what,” he said, “shall we do to the others?”
They answered, “Let them likewise suffer the final death.”
And when about the third hour came, and the saints had finished their customary prayer,
they began encouraging one another to do good. Then those cruel men came
and rushed at the saints to devour them alive. But when the saints saw them, they went joyfully toward the crown of suffering.
One of them was of noble ancestry and renowned for his family,
named Bassoes, radiant with grace and a true soldier of Christ.
Rejoicing and filled with God’s grace, he said to his companions, “Stand firm, brothers, and bravely
for Christ against this vile man, so that we may enjoy eternal glory. Let us set out on our beloved [?] path.
Let none of us remain behind. But if anyone does not have a steadfast mind, let him separate himself from us.
Do you not know, my lords, that in our own land, though renowned for my family, high in rank, and very rich,
I ran [?], competed, and labored in the public arena? Back then, for the sake of wealth and human praise
and fleeting pleasure, I strove. But now, how much more for the sake of the heavenly King!
Therefore, brothers, let us all be strong, and let us not prove inferior to Christ’s martyrs, but let us suffer bravely for him.
I know this, brothers: no human being is free from death. So, if death lies before us,
let us escape eternal death. For the death we face now is short-lived.
It is called sleep for the righteous. So let no one fall behind the company, so that we may all alike receive the crown
from God, the giver of rewards, and our Lord Jesus Christ. O mind filled with the true faith!
O ladder reaching heaven! O courageous mind! For at the judgment seat of the persecutor
your resolve did not waver, but became still stronger. First, having torn away from the company
Constantine the patrician, who was on earth, the cruel and merciless servants of the devil—
but he became an angel of God in heaven. Having torn his clothes,
they cut off his honored head. Then they did the same to Theophilus the chief sword-bearer,
and after him to Callistus the sword-bearer. When they came to Bassoës, Christ’s laborer,
seeing that they were tearing their clothes, he undressed himself and said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb;
naked I shall depart. Clothe me, O Christ, in your incorruptible garment.”
And when they had cut off his honored head too, they left him in the prison
where the saints were being held under guard. As they were singing the Third Hour, as was their custom,
they suddenly saw a certain power sent down to them from heaven
to give light, shining threefold, and a voice came from it: “Of the passion-bearer Bassoës
I am the light.” Many Christian men saw this and praised God,
and understood that the saint had met his end. After Christ’s martyr had met his end,
they immediately beheaded each of them there, one by one. And so the blessed ones surrendered their souls.
The forty-two holy martyrs met their end on March 7, when the Greek realm was ruled by
Michael, Theodore, and Thecla, the orthodox sovereigns. Glorifying God
and offering him a song of praise, with one soul and one mind,
they finished the race and received the crown. When the saints had met their end,
the deceitful ruler ordered another Christian to be brought, saying, “Submit to me and be of one mind with me,
or you will die horribly like these men. But if you submit to me, you will be honored in my palace,
and you will be worthy to receive great wealth and gifts from me.” Having deceived himself and been moved in his heart,
that wretched man said, “I will do your will, O king, if only I may live.”
Filled with joy, he said to him, “If you wish to convince me, I will bring you what you call the cross.
Trample it before my eyes and renounce it. If you do this, you will be my close friend.”
The wretched man said, “I will do your will, O emperor.” They brought the precious cross of Christ and laid it on the ground.
He trampled it, saying, “I renounce [?] their Christian faith, and I will be of one mind with you, O emperor.”
Oh, how did your filthy feet not grow numb? How did his hair not stand on end
with his darkened mind? Concerning this, concerning so great a thing [?], when he had already committed this lawless deed so boldly,
the Saracen nobles said to the emperor, “It is not right for him to live.
Let him too be condemned to death. For if he did not keep his own faith,
neither will he keep ours.” When they had said this, the Commander of the Faithful ordered him to be beheaded.
Oh, the misery! What cries did the wretched man utter? What thoughts did he carry in his heart
when he received his death sentence—he who had become dead even before his death?
Having lost your faith, you did not escape death either, you wretched and miserable man! What did you gain? When they had beheaded him,
he ordered his body to be thrown into the river with the bodies of the martyrs. When they had been thrown in,
the wretched man’s body immediately sank there, but the bodies of these noble martyrs floated on the surface like ships.
And like rays of sunlight, their heads came together with their own bodies toward the shore,
not wishing to be separated from them. For the Lord truly does not forsake those who love him.
And a most glorious wonder could be seen: how the bodies
of the saints were carried through the water. But it was God, O martyrs, whom you loved
and for whose sake you chose death—it was he who performed this wonder.
As the bodies of the noble martyrs were carried through the river, they came to the bank and stopped
where the saints themselves had chosen. Some of those who loved Christ took their bodies,
anointed them with myrrh, and laid them in a distinguished place. And I beseech your assembly, O martyrs,
glorious and honored, chosen servants, noble martyrs, workers trained in the true faith,
imitators of Christ, dwelling places of the Holy Spirit, bold confessors, of one mind with the angels,
servants of the Lord and Father, disciples of the Only-Begotten, havens and protectors for Christians.
Being in the kingdom of heaven, pray to God for protection from war, famine, and destruction.
Do not disregard the body of the Church as it is torn apart. Protect it in every distress.
Free the captives and pray for the sick. We who have sinned ask the Lord that we may receive forgiveness through you.
May we be strengthened to spend our remaining years in good order, reverence, and fear of God.
May we finish this lowly life of ours in peace and meet our end without fear.
For you were killed for Christ, and therefore received crowns from the Lord’s hands.
And at the time of visitation you shone more brightly than the sunlight.
For you, noble martyrs, proclaimed grace and the faith of wisdom among evildoers.
And for this reason you rejoice forever. Strengthen our kings; make our faith firm.
Protect us always, for we have you as our defenders and intercessors.
We will not fear any adversity that comes upon us, always having our hope in the Master, Christ our true God.
Do not cease to pray for us, so that we too may receive eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
To him be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
